actor: Memory capacity allocation planner, vertically integrated device and component maker
job: Routing constrained memory capacity to server customers ahead of the company's own handset lines, quarter by quarter as loading plans are set.
outcome: A handset bill of materials priced off residual capacity, keeping the phone unit's component cost above what its selling price recovers.
motivation: The server customer carries a seventy percent operating margin; the internal handset buyer does not, so allocation follows the margin.

task.who: Fab loading and product-mix planning teams in the component division
task.what: Allocate constrained memory output to server customers first
task.where: Quarterly fab loading and product-mix planning cycle
task.why: Server demand carries the higher margin per allocated bit
task.how: Capacity allocation model weighted by margin per wafer start

actor: Multi-year capacity contract manager, memory supply planning
job: Placing sixty to seventy percent of memory capacity under multi-year datacentre contracts, shrinking the pool the handset unit can still draw from.
outcome: Contracted volume large enough that redirecting bits to the internal phone business would breach agreements, making the handset cost squeeze structural.
motivation: Contracted visibility through the shortage is the asset sold to investors, and it disappears the moment committed bits get diverted internally.

task.who: Sales planning, contract management and legal counsel
task.what: Lock memory capacity under multi-year datacentre supply agreements
task.where: Customer contract negotiations and committed-volume reviews
task.why: Committed volume makes the internal squeeze structural, not discretionary
task.how: Multi-year committed-volume and pricing agreement templates

actor: Entry-tier device product planner, mass-market handset portfolio
job: Withdrawing higher-capacity memory options from cheap models rather than pricing them up, trimming the configuration ladder as component supply tightens.
outcome: A mass-market line-up shipping less memory per unit, holding segment revenue down while the handset business carries the same fixed cost.
motivation: A visible price rise at the cheap end costs volume, so the adjustment is made quietly in the specification sheet instead.

task.who: Mass-market product planning and hardware specification teams
task.what: Remove higher-capacity memory variants from entry-tier models
task.where: Regional line-up and specification sheets for mass-market models
task.why: Spec trimming hides the cost pass-through a price rise reveals
task.how: Configuration matrix revisions and regional SKU rationalisation

actor: Component procurement lead, handset hardware cost engineering
job: Negotiating the memory and component bill for the next hardware cycle against an internal supplier whose external customers bid the price up.
outcome: A locked component cost the phone unit carries into the following two reported quarters, above the level its selling prices recover.
motivation: Volume commitments must be placed before the build cycle, so the elevated price is signed for well ahead of the quarter it hits.

task.who: Hardware cost engineering and component sourcing teams
task.what: Fix memory volumes and prices for the next build cycle
task.where: Annual component sourcing and supplier price negotiation cycle
task.why: Prices signed now set the cost the segment reports later
task.how: Component cost models and committed-volume purchase agreements

actor: Flagship pricing and product cost planner, premium handset line
job: Setting the next flagship price ladder in roughly the same band as the current one while the memory line of the bill keeps climbing.
outcome: A launch that carries the higher component cost into its strongest season without a price rise large enough to recover it.
motivation: A rise big enough to cover the memory bill would cost more volume than it recovers, so the gap stays in the operating line.

task.who: Product marketing, pricing committee and finance planning
task.what: Set the next flagship launch price ladder
task.where: Launch pricing committee and regional price-band review
task.why: A cost-covering rise would cost more volume than it recovers
task.how: Regional price-band models and competitive elasticity analysis

actor: Flagship launch programme manager, handset hardware engineering
job: Bringing the next flagship to market on the same constrained memory supply, through the quarter the phone unit counts as its strongest.
outcome: A flagship launch landing in the seasonally strongest quarter without lowering the unit's component bill, so the loss survives its best season.
motivation: A launch date already announced to carriers and retail partners is far more costly to move than to hit with a worse bill.

task.who: Hardware engineering and launch programme management
task.what: Ship the next flagship on constrained memory supply
task.where: Launch readiness gates and mass-production ramp schedule
task.why: An announced launch is costlier to move than to absorb
task.how: Mass-production ramp milestones and supplier allocation commitments

actor: Segment reporting and investor disclosure lead, consolidated results
job: Preparing the segment tables and results commentary that put the phone and network unit's operating result on the record each quarter.
outcome: Three consecutive published segment tables showing the mobile and networks operating line in the red, which is what the claim is read against.
motivation: Segment disclosure is a filing obligation, so the result is published on schedule regardless of how badly it reads.

task.who: Investor relations, corporate finance and disclosure teams
task.what: Publish the mobile and networks segment operating result
task.where: Quarterly earnings release, results call and regulatory filing
task.why: The claim is settled only by the company's own segment table
task.how: Segment reporting pack, earnings deck and regulatory filing
